papers.title: Canonical lymphocyte chemokine receptors CXCR3 and CXCR5 modulate neuronal autophagy.
papers.summary: This paper investigates chemokine receptors CXCR3 and CXCR5, which are typically known for their roles in immune cell trafficking, and finds that they also play a role in neurons. The study shows that these receptors can influence autophagy, the process by which cells degrade and recycle their own components, specifically in neurons. This suggests a previously unrecognized link between immune signaling molecules and neuronal self-maintenance pathways.
papers.why: Since the abstract is minimal, it's unclear if this touches spatial or interneuron-specific aspects, but the core finding that chemokine receptors modulate neuronal autophagy is directly relevant to the project's focus on autophagy mechanisms in neurons.

papers.title: CellART: a unified framework for extracting single-cell information from high-resolution spatial transcriptomics
papers.summary: CellART is a computational framework designed to extract single-cell level information from high-resolution spatial transcriptomics data. It likely integrates image segmentation, transcript assignment, and cell typing into a unified pipeline to accurately resolve individual cells within complex tissue. This addresses a common challenge in spatial transcriptomics where transcript-to-cell assignment is imprecise, especially in densely packed tissue like brain.
papers.why: Accurate single-cell resolution from spatial transcriptomics is essential for reliably identifying interneuron subtypes and their perineuronal net microenvironments in brain tissue, and such AI-driven pipelines directly parallel the deep learning image/data analysis approaches central to this PhD project.

papers.title: SPRINT enables spatial proteomic profile reconstruction through multimodal fusion of histology and transcriptomics
papers.summary: SPRINT is a new computational method that predicts spatial proteomic profiles by combining histology images with spatial transcriptomics data. It uses multimodal fusion techniques, likely deep learning, to infer protein distributions across tissue sections without needing direct spatial proteomics measurements. This approach could make it easier to generate proteomic maps from more commonly available histology and transcriptomic datasets.
papers.why: This tool could help integrate spatial transcriptomics with inferred proteomic data in brain tissue, potentially enriching multimodal analyses of mitophagy pathways, interneuron subtypes, and perineuronal net composition without requiring separate costly proteomics experiments.
papers.figure: Figure showing the multimodal fusion architecture and workflow of SPRINT alongside example predicted vs. ground-truth spatial proteomic maps.

papers.title: Augmenting intracellular amino acid pools suppresses the phenotypes of autophagy-deficient cells.
papers.summary: This paper investigates whether boosting intracellular amino acid levels can compensate for the loss of autophagy in cells. The researchers likely find that supplying extra amino acids helps restore normal cell function even when autophagy, the cell's recycling process, is disabled. This suggests that one of autophagy's key roles is to maintain a sufficient supply of amino acids for cellular processes.
papers.why: Since autophagy and mitophagy are central to neuronal health, understanding how amino acid supplementation can rescue autophagy-deficient phenotypes may reveal alternative therapeutic strategies for neurons with impaired autophagic flux, which is highly relevant to interneuron and perineuronal net degeneration studies.

papers.title: Redox state of Protein Kinase A RIα coordinates lysosomal calcium signaling and mitochondrial homeostasis.
papers.summary: This paper investigates how the redox (oxidation) state of a regulatory subunit of Protein Kinase A, called RIα, acts as a sensor that links cellular oxidative conditions to calcium release from lysosomes. This lysosomal calcium signaling in turn influences mitochondrial function and overall cellular homeostasis. The study establishes a molecular pathway connecting redox status, organelle communication, and calcium signaling that could be relevant to how cells maintain quality control under stress.
papers.why: Since mitophagy relies on coordinated calcium signaling between lysosomes and mitochondria, this mechanism could inform how redox-sensitive lysosomal-mitochondrial crosstalk regulates neuronal mitophagy and organelle quality control in brain cells under study.

papers.title: LAPTM5 correlates with RPE senescence and subretinal fibrosis through the LAPTM5-WWP2-OPTN mitophagy cascade and cGAS/STING activation in a D-galactose-induced aging model.
papers.summary: This paper studies LAPTM5, a protein involved in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cell aging in a mouse model treated with D-galactose to induce accelerated aging. The researchers found that LAPTM5 works with WWP2 and OPTN to regulate mitophagy (the clearance of damaged mitochondria), and that disruption of this pathway leads to activation of the cGAS/STING immune signaling axis. This cascade is linked to RPE cell senescence and scarring (fibrosis) beneath the retina.
papers.why: This work demonstrates a concrete mitophagy signaling cascade (LAPTM5-WWP2-OPTN) linked to cGAS/STING activation and cellular senescence, offering a mechanistic template that could inform how similar mitophagy-immune crosstalk might operate in aging neurons or glial cells in the brain.

papers.title: SIRT7-Mediated H2BK120 Succinylation Drives Aberrant Mitophagy in Sepsis-Associated Cognitive Dysfunction.
papers.summary: This study investigates how sepsis leads to cognitive problems by looking at a specific brain protein modification process. The researchers found that an enzyme called SIRT7 controls a chemical tag (succinylation) on histone H2B, which in turn affects how brain cells break down their damaged mitochondria (mitophagy). When this process goes wrong during sepsis, it appears to contribute to the brain dysfunction seen in sepsis patients.
papers.why: This paper directly examines mitophagy dysregulation in neurons through an epigenetic mechanism, offering a potential molecular pathway relevant to the mitophagy-focused arm of the PhD project even though it lacks spatial omics or AI components.
papers.figure: A figure showing colocalization of SIRT7, H2BK120succinylation marks, and mitophagy markers (e.g., LC3/PINK1/Parkin) in neurons from septic versus control brain tissue.

papers.title: MCAT-mediated mitochondrial fatty acid metabolism regulates Lauren subtype divergence and suppresses gastric cancer progression through ROS/P53-dependent mitophagy and ferroptosis.
papers.summary: This paper studies MCAT, an enzyme involved in mitochondrial fatty acid synthesis, and shows it influences gastric cancer subtype and progression. The mechanism involves MCAT promoting mitophagy and ferroptosis through ROS and P53 signaling, which suppresses tumor growth. It links a specific mitochondrial metabolic pathway to cell death and cancer subtype divergence in a non-neuronal, oncology context.
papers.why: While this is a gastric cancer study, the mechanistic focus on ROS/P53-dependent mitophagy could offer transferable pathway insights relevant to mitophagy regulation in neurons, though the tissue and disease context is largely unrelated to the core neuroscience focus.
papers.figure: A figure showing the proposed mechanistic pathway linking MCAT, mitochondrial fatty acid metabolism, ROS/P53 signaling, mitophagy, and ferroptosis.
